clinicalPearls: SPG9 is caused by variants in ALDH18A1, which encodes the mitochondrial enzyme delta-1-pyrroline-5-carboxylate synthase (P5CS); both autosomal dominant (SPG9A) and autosomal recessive (SPG9B) forms exist.
It is a complicated HSP, and bilateral cataracts are a hallmark that should prompt consideration of this subtype when they accompany spastic paraparesis.
The original phenotype combined spastic paraplegia, cataracts, gastro-oesophageal reflux with vomiting and a motor neuropathy or distal amyotrophy.
Short stature and skeletal abnormalities are recognised accompanying features.
Recessive presentations tend to be earlier in onset and more likely to include developmental delay and intellectual disability than dominant ones.
Because ALDH18A1 sits at the head of proline and ornithine synthesis, the same gene also causes cutis laxa syndromes, so overlapping connective-tissue features may be seen.
Plasma amino acids may show low proline, ornithine, citrulline and arginine, but these can be subtle and can normalise in the fed state.
A slit-lamp examination for lens opacities is a simple and high-yield step when this diagnosis is suspected.
reference.pathophysiology: SPG9 results from variants in ALDH18A1, encoding delta-1-pyrroline-5-carboxylate synthase (P5CS), a bifunctional mitochondrial enzyme that converts glutamate to glutamate-5-semialdehyde and its cyclised form pyrroline-5-carboxylate. This is the rate-limiting, committed step in the de novo biosynthesis of proline and ornithine, and hence feeds the downstream production of citrulline and arginine through the urea cycle. Impaired P5CS activity depletes these amino acids, disturbing collagen and elastin metabolism (accounting for the connective-tissue and cutis laxa overlap) and compromising neuronal and lens homeostasis. Dominant variants are thought to act through a dominant-negative effect on the enzyme complex, whereas recessive variants cause more complete loss of function with correspondingly earlier and more severe, often cognitively involved, disease; the degenerative burden falls preferentially on the long corticospinal tracts, producing the spastic paraparesis.
additionalDifferentials: Other complicated HSP subtypes presenting with cataracts or amyotrophy
Cerebrotendinous xanthomatosis (juvenile cataracts with neurological decline)
Cutis laxa syndromes including de Barsy syndrome (allelic ALDH18A1 disease)
Distal hereditary motor neuropathies where amyotrophy dominates the picture
additionalInvestigations: Plasma amino acid profile examining proline, ornithine, citrulline and arginine
Nerve conduction studies and electromyography for a motor axonal neuropathy
Molecular analysis of ALDH18A1 with attention to dominant versus recessive inheritance
MRI of the brain and spinal cord
Skeletal survey and growth assessment where short stature or deformity is present
redFlags: Failure to thrive or feeding difficulty with significant gastro-oesophageal reflux and vomiting
Rapidly progressive distal amyotrophy and weakness
Signs suggestive of hyperammonaemia or metabolic decompensation in severe neonatal presentations
Visual deterioration from progressive cataract requiring ophthalmic intervention
reference.prognosis: The course is variable; recessive disease with early onset and cognitive involvement tends to be more disabling, whereas dominant disease may be milder and more slowly progressive. The associated cataracts and neuropathy add to long-term morbidity even when the paraparesis progresses slowly.
pitfalls: Relying on a single fed-state amino acid measurement, which may appear normal despite the underlying enzyme defect
Overlooking the connective-tissue and cutis laxa overlap that points to ALDH18A1
Failing to distinguish autosomal dominant from recessive forms, which alters counselling and expected severity
Attributing the cataracts to an unrelated cause and missing the unifying diagnosis
references: Bradley and Daroff's Neurology in Clinical Practice
Adams and Victor's Principles of Neurology
management: No specific therapy corrects the P5CS enzyme defect; treat lower-limb spasticity with oral baclofen or tizanidine, focal botulinum toxin and physiotherapy with orthoses and mobility aids
Refer for ophthalmology assessment and cataract surgery, a hallmark of this complicated subtype
Manage gastro-oesophageal reflux and vomiting with proton pump inhibitors, upright positioning and feeding support to reduce aspiration risk
Support the associated motor neuropathy, distal amyotrophy and, in recessive early-onset disease, developmental delay with rehabilitation and educational input
Surveillance of growth, skeletal deformity and short stature in children, alongside monitoring of neurological progression
Multidisciplinary care linking neurology, ophthalmology, gastroenterology, physiotherapy and clinical genetics
Offer genetic counselling, distinguishing autosomal dominant (SPG9A) from recessive (SPG9B) inheritance for family risk assessment
